frontmatter.title: D1 Future climate and weather files

children.value: This chapter is being reworked and may change substantially.
Future climate changes and given the life span of buildings, they need to be designed for that. This chapter gives an overview of the climate challenges.
D1.2 What is in a weather file

children.label: D1.2 What is in a weather file

children.value: A weather file holds one year of hourly outdoor conditions for one location: dry-bulb temperature, humidity, direct normal, diffuse and global horizontal radiation, wind speed and direction, and cloud cover. Three abbreviations recur:

, typical meteorological year: the general term for one artificial year assembled from twelve typical months taken from many years of data. It represents average weather, not extremes. The data behind it can be measurements or, as in the Annex 80 files (section D1.4), climate model output.

, design reference year: the Danish national typical year, published by DMI (section D1.3). It is assembled in the same way, but only from months measured at one station and selected with the method of ISO 15927-4, and it is the year used to show compliance with the Danish building regulations. A TMY from another source for the same location therefore differs from the DRY in both the data and the selection method.

Weather files come in many different file formats. The best known is EPW, the EnergyPlus weather file, which is a text format with 8 header lines followed by 8,760 hourly rows. Most building simulation tools read it.
The DRY files can be downloaded as EPW or CSV from
D1.3 The Danish design reference year - DMI

children.label: D1.3 The Danish design reference year - DMI

children.value: A reference year is one artificial year of hourly weather. It is assembled from twelve real calendar months, each picked from a longer measured record as the most typical month of its kind. Danish Meteorological Institute (DMI) selects the months with the Finkelstein–Schafer method of ISO 15927-4. The method compares the distribution of daily values in each candidate month with the distribution for all years, using temperature, global radiation and humidity as primary parameters and wind and precipitation as secondary ones.
Denmark has two generations of design reference year (DRY), both for the DMI station at Sjælsmark north of Copenhagen, with solar radiation measured at DTU in Lyngby:
, the reference used in building regulations until now.
reference years for three emission scenarios:
RCP is Representative Concentration Pathway and reflect future greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere:
Each RCP scenario was projected for four periods:
DMI considers RCP4.5 the most likely scenario
, as it corresponds to about 2.7 °C of global warming by the end of the century
Climate models give only daily temperature and precipitation, not the hourly radiation and humidity a simulation needs. So DMI used the projected daily values to

months from the measured 2014–2023 record: for each calendar month the measured month whose temperature distribution best matches the projection is picked. Where two months match equally well, the one that also matches the projected precipitation best is chosen. Every hour in a future file is therefore real, measured weather from the last decade.

Enthalpy is the annual mean total specific enthalpy of the outdoor air per kg dry air,

children.value: found from air temperature, relative humidity and pressure.

Enthalpy expresses the total energy content of the atmosphere (latent and sensible heat). In a building context, it indicates the increased work load on a chiller that needs to both cool the air, as well as shed the water content.
The UTCI column is explained in the section on heat stress indices below.
A big step has already happened.
reference year raises the mean temperature by about 1.5 °C and cuts the hours below 0 °C by more than half, yet
Hours above 26 °C rise from 37 today to 80–90 around mid-century.
Global radiation stays at about 1,020–1,040 kWh/m² and mean relative humidity at 81–83 %. Solar gains in the future files are those of today.

The 2080–2099 file is no warmer than 2055–2074; the two differ only in January, May and October. Because every future month must be a measured month from 2014–2023, the files can never be hotter than the hottest month of that decade.
Air temperature alone does not tell how hot it feels outdoors. Sun, wind and humidity matter as much, and a heat stress index combines them into one number.

is the index used in this chapter. It is the air temperature of a reference environment that gives the same physiological strain as the actual one, for a person walking at 4 km/h. The reference environment has 50 % relative humidity, almost no wind and no radiation beyond that of the air temperature. The inputs are air temperature, humidity, wind speed and mean radiant temperature. Here the mean radiant temperature is that of a person standing in the open, found from the direct and diffuse solar radiation in the weather file (the SolarCal method of ASHRAE 55). The tables count the hours with UTCI above 26 °C, which is where moderate heat stress begins.
UTCI is an outdoor index. Its ten stress classes
, is built on the same idea as UTCI and uses the same inputs, but with an indoor reference environment and a simpler body model. Moderate heat stress starts at about 29 °C

, the wet-bulb globe temperature, is a weighted mean of the natural wet-bulb, globe and air temperatures. It is the index of occupational and sports heat limits. It needs measured wet-bulb and globe temperatures, so from a weather file it can only be estimated

:::{admonition} Rules of thumb
:class: tip
- Use the current DRY for energy-frame compliance and for sizing heating.
- Check summer comfort with at least one future file as well, since a 2025 building will meet a 2050 climate.
- A reference year is built from *typical* months. DMI itself says it is not suited for sizing against extreme events such as overheating. Stress-test the design with a heat-wave file (section 5).
:::
The IEA EBC Annex 80 project made a set of Copenhagen files
from the MPI-REMO regional climate model (EURO-CORDEX): typical meteorological years (TMY) for:
and three heat-wave years picked from 2041–2060 under RCP8.5 and bias-adjusted against observations from 2001–2019.
Unlike the DRY files, these are model output, not measured months, so they can be hotter than anything seen so far.

In the typical years the Annex 80 files warm in both seasons (

): the winter median rises from 4.2 °C to 6.2 °C and the summer median from 14.1 °C to 15.8 °C. The heat-wave years have almost the same summer median as the typical year of the same period. They differ in the warm tail, which is longest in the most severe year, with 192 hours above 26 °C against 82 in the typical year.

*The heat-wave file “longest” (2045) has no solar radiation from 1 to 14 August: global, direct and diffuse radiation are zero in all 336 hours, while temperature and humidity run on normally. The gap lies inside the heat wave the file was made for (15 July to 20 August 2045). Its annual global radiation is therefore about 90 kWh/m² too low, and its UTCI hours are underestimated. Use this file for temperature and humidity only, and the “most intense” or “most severe” file where solar gains matter. The three heat-wave files also contain 4–6 corrupt hours of global and diffuse radiation (values far above 1,400 W/m²); these were removed and interpolated before the table was computed.

Heat waves raise mortality, mainly through cardiovascular and respiratory strain, and the old and the sick are most at risk. The hot summer of 2018 caused about 380 additional deaths in Finland, and the heat-related mortality risk in Helsinki was about 2.5 times that of the surrounding rural areas

The summer of 2026 gave similar numbers in western Europe. All three are provisional estimates from the national health agencies. In France, 5,764 more people than expected died during the heat wave of 17 June to 2 July, an excess of 36 %
. In England, 2,877 deaths were associated with two hot spells in May and June
. In Spain, more than 5,200 deaths were attributed to heat between May and August, the highest number since monitoring began in 2015

REVIEW: the three 2026 figures above are provisional agency estimates, not journal publications. France (Santé publique France, 22 July 2026) is all-cause excess mortality; England (UKHSA interim report, 30 July 2026) is modelled heat-associated deaths; Spain is the MoMo estimate of Instituto de Salud Carlos III as reported by Meteored, a secondary source. Final figures are expected late 2026 (France, Spain) and early 2027 (England).
A reference year is assembled from typical months, so it contains no real heat wave. The Annex 80 project therefore produced separate heat-wave years.
They are the three years of 2041–2060 with the longest, the most intense (hottest) and the most severe (longest and hottest combined) heat wave.
compares them with the typical years.
Hot days and tropical nights in the Copenhagen weather files, computed from the EPW files. A tropical night has a minimum above 20 °C between 21:00 and 09:00.
Warm nights are the real problem. Night ventilation removes heat in proportion to the airflow times the temperature difference between indoor and outdoor air (
). When the night stays above 20 °C, that difference is only a few kelvin, so the thermal mass is not emptied and the next day starts warmer. After a few such days the building has no reserve left.
Simulations of Finnish apartment buildings without cooling show the result
. The heat wave of 2018 had 24 days above 25 °C and 5 tropical nights, and gave about 10,000 degree-hours above 27 °C indoors.

The same heat wave moved to the climate of 2050 has 15 tropical nights and gives about 14,000 degree-hours above 27 °C, and the degree-hours above 32 °C, a health risk threshold, triple from about 1,000 to 3,000. Openable windows were the most effective passive measure, but only a cooling unit removed the overheating completely.
The summer of 2018 was a Nordic heat-wave summer. To see how it compares, July and August of DRY 2011–2023 were replaced by DMI observations from Sjælsmark (station 06188), 1 July to 31 August 2018.
Hourly mean air temperature, relative humidity, pressure, global radiation, wind, cloud cover and precipitation from the DMI open data API. Dew point is computed from temperature and humidity.
DMI measures only global radiation. Direct and diffuse radiation are split from it with the Erbs model
. On the original July and August of the DRY, the split gives about 10 % less direct and 5 % more diffuse radiation than DMI’s own values.
The jumps in temperature and humidity at 1 July and 1 September are spread over 13 hours. All other months are the original DRY.

The 2018 heat wave was on par with the Annex 80 “most intense” year 2055. Their summers have almost the same mean (18.2 and 18.0 °C), the same 99th percentile (29.2 and 29.1 °C) and about the same degree-hours above 26 °C (217 and 194 Kh). It was far from the “most severe” year 2054, which has nearly twice the degree-hours (399 Kh), 192 instead of 125 hours above 26 °C and 42 instead of 29 days above 25 °C. The summer of 2018 is therefore a realistic heat wave for the 2050s, but not the worst case.
The urban heat island intensity is the air temperature difference

children.html: ΔTUHI=Turban−Trural\Delta T_\mathrm{UHI} = T_\mathrm{urban} - T_\mathrm{rural}ΔTUHI​=Turban​−Trural​

children.value: . It is mainly a night-time effect and peaks a few hours before sunrise on calm, clear summer nights. The causes:
brick, concrete and asphalt store solar heat during the day and release it at night.
street canyons see little of the cold night sky, so long-wave cooling is reduced.
sealed surfaces drain rain away instead of evaporating it.
buildings reduce convective cooling and mixing.
In Denmark the effect is modest but not negligible.

shows it for the four largest Danish cities. On the 3 % warmest days of the year, Copenhagen is on average 1.5–2 K warmer than its rural surroundings at night, and on some nights close to 3 K. The difference almost disappears around 09:00. The other three cities stay at about 1 K
. In four Finnish cities the mean intensity is 0.5–1.2 K, peaking at about 1.5 K around 05:00 in Helsinki

For comparison, a model study of 100 European cities at 100 m resolution for 2008–2017 finds an average heat island indicator of 1.43 °C. Green areas and unsealed soil already lower it by 0.45 °C on average, and more of both could lower it by about another 0.5 °C

The effect of urban heat islands is more pronounced with future climate, but the magnitude will probably remain the same or even decrease a little as global radiation drops, and mitigating actions are implemented like more green areas in the built environment. Cities are projected to warm by about 1.9 K by 2100 under an intermediate emission scenario
, while in Brussels the summer night-time heat island stays at about 3.1–3.2 K up to the 2060s under both RCP4.5 and RCP8.5
